blocks.text: In all the aqueous solutions, the concentration of H⁺ and OH⁻ are too low to be conveniently expressed and used in calculations. In 1909, Sorenson, a Danish biochemist, introduced the term pH and pOH. So, the scales of pH and pOH were developed. These two quantities can be calculated as:

blocks.title: Interesting Information!
blocks.text: Solutions of negative pH and having values more than 14 are also known.
The value of pH normally varies between 0 → 14 at 25 °C.
The pH values of some familiar aqueous solutions are shown in Figure 9.1. This table can help you to understand the acidic or basic nature of commonly used solutions.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 9.1
blocks.problem: In a solution, the pH is 9.2. Determine the ionic product of water Kw at 25°C.
steps: Calculate the pOH from the pH: pOH = 14 − pH; pOH = 14 − 9.2; pOH = 4.8
Find the concentration of H⁺ and OH⁻, Taking antilog of pH and pOH

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The pH gives the H⁺ concentration, not OH⁻: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ = 10⁻⁹·² ≈ 6.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ M. The OH⁻ concentration comes from the pOH: [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁴·⁸ ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ M.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 9.2
blocks.problem: The ionic product of water at a certain temperature is Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 ºC. If the concentration of H⁺ ions in a solution is 1.0 × 10⁻⁷M. Calculate the concentration of OH⁻ ions, the pH and pOH of the solution.
steps: Use the expression for Kw: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
Substitute the known values of Kw and the concentration of H⁺: 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ = (1.0 × 10⁻⁷) [OH⁻]
Solve for the concentration of OH⁻: [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M; this is the value used for pOH = 7.
